# Bootstrapping an AI-Native Ecosystem {#sec-bootstrapping-ecosystem}

::: {.epigraph}
> "The more designers involved in using the new methods, and the better they are able to communicate with each other, the faster the process of cultural integration runs."
>
> — Lynn Conway, *The MPC Adventures* [@Conway1981MPCAdventures, p. 2]
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
**Governing question:** *What must exist beyond any one team for AI-native architecture claims to become comparable, and how much of it can a single team adopt without waiting?*

**Core thesis:** *Shared data, implementation paths, comparisons, and teaching resources let AI-native design become accessible and cumulative, while individual teams can begin with rigorous local practice.*
:::

An architecture group can retain failed tool runs, measure its workflow costs, and tighten its baseline comparisons without waiting for a community standard. These practices make its own work easier to examine, but local discipline alone cannot make another organization's parser interpret an exported record correctly, establish a neutral public benchmark, or open access to a semiconductor fabrication line.

That boundary appears the moment an AI-native architecture claim leaves the team's own repository (@fig-ch12-cover-map). A claim that a candidate design transfers cleanly to another toolchain depends on shared record contracts. A claim that it closes timing at a target process node depends on qualified process design kits (PDKs) and fabrication paths. A claim that it beats competing architectures on a public leaderboard depends on neutral benchmark rules and a way to resolve disputes. Independent comparison therefore requires agreement on what records mean and access to the tools and checks that produced the result.

The same records and implementation paths can support teaching when maintained examples let students construct alternatives, test design hypotheses, and investigate failures. A course can begin this work locally; shared teaching artifacts would let other courses reproduce and extend it. Whether the proposed infrastructure makes claims across organizations more comparable remains an empirical question. Local engineering discipline does not have to wait for the answer.

![**Local engineering practices proceed immediately, while cross-organizational claims require shared infrastructure.** The top tier shows practices an individual team can enforce inside its own repository (lineage tracking, negative-result retention, and matched baselines), whereas the three lower branches trace the external community schemas, fabrication shuttles, and consortium rules required when claims cross organizational boundaries.](images/ch12-cover-map.svg){#fig-ch12-cover-map width="100%" fig-alt="Overview diagram distinguishing unilateral local engineering practices from shared community infrastructure dependencies. A top panel details immediate local capabilities in lineage tracking, negative-result retention, and baseline matching, while three lower branches detail external requirements for cross-team comparisons, physical or silicon signoff, and public benchmark programs."}

## Local Practice and Shared Infrastructure {#sec-staging-sequence}

In 1979, Lynn Conway's Multi-Project Chip (MPC79) run joined a teachable design method to shared fabrication access. Mead and Conway's scalable $\lambda$-based design rules let university designers work with common layout abstractions; Xerox PARC then combined the layouts they sent over ARPANET into shared mask sets. The run fabricated 82 student and research projects. The later MOSIS service kept the multi-project wafer model going by sharing fixed fabrication costs across participants [@MeadConway1980VLSI; @Conway1981MPCAdventures; @MOSIS1981VLSI]. The advance depended on both what an individual designer could learn and what institutions made possible together.

AI-native design faces a related coordination problem. A learned placer may depend on one electronic design automation (EDA) tool version, standard-cell library, or process deck. Another group cannot reproduce its result merely by downloading model weights. It needs the applicable inputs, tools, and rights to use them, as well as agreement on what the returned measurements mean. Shared interfaces, accessible implementation paths, and neutral comparisons address different parts of that dependency.

A team can begin before those agreements exist. It can identify its artifacts and tool versions, retain failed attempts, protect evaluation criteria, run credible conventional baselines, and report compute, license, and human costs. These practices cost storage and engineering effort, but the team can adopt them on its own authority. Cross-team schemas, shared fabrication access, and public benchmark rules instead require other organizations to participate.

The boundary in @fig-ch12-cover-map also reveals dependencies among the proposed shared efforts. These efforts can proceed together, but a public benchmark cannot require a physical check that its intended participants have no means to run.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Anchor AI-Native Design Systems in Open Foundations"}
**The principle:** Develop shared interfaces, reference paths, and comparison practices around the checks that independent teams need to perform. Open schemas, accessible implementation flows, neutral benchmarks, and qualified failure repositories are proposed ways to make that work possible.

**The application:** Begin local cost, provenance, failure-retention, and comparison practices now. Build shared infrastructure around the work another team needs to interpret, reproduce, or extend a result.
:::

## Shared Data Schemas and Tool Contracts {#sec-standardized-data-lineage}

Consider what happens when a retained study record reaches another team's tool flow. A reported timing slack value is useful only if the record also states its units, operating corner, and constraint status. When an optimizer exchanges spatial coordinates or power-domain declarations through ad hoc strings, a downstream parser can accept the input while silently assigning it the wrong physical meaning. If missing measurements are encoded as zeros, a surrogate model can mistake an unmeasured wire delay or resistance for a measured zero and rank a flawed candidate too favorably. Before a receiving model can use the record, the participating organizations must agree on what the exchanged state means (@sec-loop-patterns-across-stack).

An engineer can sometimes repair an ambiguous handoff by consulting the colleague who produced it. An automated workflow cannot depend on that conversation at every boundary. The tool contracts developed in @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces must therefore retain their meaning when exported to another organization, including when that organization uses a different parser or tool version.

The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) 1666 SystemC standard shows that organizations can agree on common modeling semantics [@IEEE2011SystemC1666]. A shared interface for AI-native design could coordinate three existing kinds of information:

- **Problem formulations** state the permitted changes, fixed requirements, comparator, and acceptance criteria so that another team can reconstruct the question being tested.
- **Artifact lineage** identifies the inputs and transformations behind a result, including the tool and environment versions needed to interpret or reproduce it.
- **Environmental contracts** specify input prerequisites, returned quantities and statuses, and the assumptions that limit each check.

These records would surround established design formats rather than replace them. A circuit representation describes the hardware; a workflow record explains what a tool did to that representation and under which conditions. Shared schemas need compatibility tests that exercise those meanings, not merely confirm that a file parses. For the timing example, a test should distinguish a measured zero slack from an absent measurement and reject an unrecognized unit or status instead of silently assigning a default.

Agreement on record meanings leaves identity and access as separate concerns. A cryptographic hash identifies exact bytes, and an authenticated supply-chain attestation binds a named issuer to a statement about how those bytes were produced [@SLSA2026Framework]. Neither establishes circuit correctness or grants permission to share the underlying design. Teams may exchange selected metadata while withholding cell libraries or proprietary netlists. A disclosure review must then judge what the released records reveal in combination and name the checks that another group cannot repeat.

Even a well-specified schema gains traction only if design teams require compatible exports from the tools they procure and contribute conformance tests that check how those exports are interpreted. If enough customers ask for the same exports, teams could stop maintaining separate wrappers and compare tool behavior on identical inputs, provided the schema's maintainers keep the compatibility tests current as tools and schemas evolve. Agreement on timing and layout records solves only half of the cross-team validation problem, however. Independent researchers also need legal and technical access to the physical implementation flows that produce those records.

## Open Implementation Paths and Silicon Access {#sec-precompetitive-infrastructure}

A timing or power result depends on device models, cell libraries, wiring rules, and the layout produced under them. A process-node label alone does not supply those inputs. Foundry agreements often restrict their distribution, leaving an academic laboratory unable to repeat a commercial implementation study even when its architecture and method are public. Another authorized industrial team may be able to review the result, but that remains distinct from open reproduction.

Open process design kits narrow this access gap. SkyWater SKY130 (130\ nm CMOS), IHP SG13G2 (130\ nm BiCMOS), and GlobalFoundries GF180MCU (180\ nm) expose device models and design rules for research on manufacturable processes [@SkyWater2020SKY130PDK; @IHPOpenPDK; @GlobalFoundriesGF180MCUOpenPDK]. Together with open synthesis, layout, and timing tools, they let researchers inspect and version more of an implementation flow. Fabrication still requires a PDK release and checks accepted by the chosen service; an open kit does not make every release production-qualified.

The available paths support different claims. A predictive kit such as ASAP7 models projected scaling trends without targeting a manufacturing line [@ClarkEtAl2016ASAP7]. A qualified implementation flow checks a design against a named process's models and rules. Measurements on fabricated devices test behavior within the measured operating conditions. Comparing results across these paths can reveal model error, but a mature-node measurement or predictive-kit estimate does not establish advanced-node signoff. Shared infrastructure should make each path accessible and record what that path can actually test.

Multi-project wafer (MPW) shuttles extend that access to fabrication by dividing fixed mask and wafer costs among participants. Following the MPC79 and MOSIS model, educational shuttles now draw thousands of design submissions at mature nodes (@fig-ch12-money-plot-tapeout-cost-collapse).

![**Open mature-node shuttles have drawn thousands of design submissions.** Designs submitted per Tiny Tapeout run on SkyWater SKY130, IHP SG13G2, and GlobalFoundries GF180MCU (bars, hatched by process), with the cumulative total reaching 4,026 across 22 runs in an August 2026 catalog snapshot (line) [@TinyTapeoutRunCatalog]. Counts include test shuttles and runs not yet delivered; they measure participation, not fabricated or working silicon, and say nothing about advanced-node signoff.](images/fig-shuttle-cost-democratization){#fig-ch12-money-plot-tapeout-cost-collapse width="80%" fig-alt="Bar chart with a cumulative line of design submissions per Tiny Tapeout shuttle run from 2022 to 2026. Bars for 22 runs range from about 30 to 547 designs, distinguished by fill pattern for the SkyWater, IHP, and GlobalFoundries processes, and the cumulative line rises from 152 to 4,026 designs."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
import json as _json12tt
from pathlib import Path as _Path12tt
import _python.plots as _ap12tt

_tt17 = _json12tt.loads(
    (_Path12tt(_ap12tt.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
     / "data" / "studies" / "17-silicon-report-coverage" / "summary.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
)
tt17_macros = _tt17["population_macro_rows"]
tt17_with_fb = _tt17["macros_with_any_public_feedback"]
tt17_with_pct = f"{_tt17['macro_feedback_presence_percent']:.1f}"
tt17_no_fb = _tt17["macros_without_public_feedback"]
tt17_no_pct = f"{100 - _tt17['macro_feedback_presence_percent']:.1f}"
tt17_records = _tt17["community_feedback_records"]
```

Full-reticle mask tooling at leading-edge nodes is estimated in the tens of millions of dollars [@Patel2022MaskSetCosts], whereas multiplexed open-process tiles lower the entry cost for a small digital design to a few hundred dollars [@TinyTapeout2025TTSky25aSubmitted].[^fn-tinytapeout-architecture-c12] That access lets students and researchers bring up a circuit, exercise it, and compare its measured behavior with pre-silicon predictions. Shared pins, die area, clocking, and instrumentation limit which experiments a vehicle can support, so choosing the shuttle is part of designing the experiment.

Wafer access does not guarantee that those comparisons are made or published. The growth in @fig-ch12-money-plot-tapeout-cost-collapse measures participation, not working silicon. Several plotted runs had not yet delivered chips at the snapshot date, and public bring-up reporting remains voluntary. Across all `{python} tt17_macros` macros on the delivered Tiny Tapeout 06 (`TT06`) shuttle [@TinyTapeout2026TT06Feedback], `{python} tt17_with_fb` macros (`{python} tt17_with_pct`%) have any public community feedback entry (`{python} tt17_records` records in total), while `{python} tt17_no_fb` macros (`{python} tt17_no_pct`%) have no public community feedback entry. Missing reports are not verified failures. Programs that provide wafer space therefore also need ways to retain measurements and enough test context for others to use them.

[^fn-tinytapeout-architecture-c12]: **Multiplexed open-shuttle tiles**: Educational shuttles achieve substantial cost reductions by tiling hundreds of independent digital designs onto a single shared silicon die. A centralized digital multiplexer connects the shared clock, reset, and a small set of input, output, and bidirectional pins to one selected design at a time, restricting digital submissions to modest frequencies (tens of megahertz), small standard-cell counts, and low-speed interfaces without dedicated high-speed pads. Some shuttles also offer analog tiles with a few dedicated pins.

Useful measurements also require instrumentation. A research vehicle might provide power-monitored rails, ring oscillators, and voltage-droop monitors to characterize timing and power behavior across voltage and temperature.[^fn-ring-oscillators-c12] Those facilities must be designed and qualified; booking wafer space does not supply them. Common characterization structures and retained test procedures could let several groups compare model error under known conditions.

[^fn-ring-oscillators-c12]: **On-chip ring oscillators and droop monitors for silicon characterization**: A ring oscillator is an on-chip test structure consisting of an odd number of inverting logic gates in a closed feedback loop whose natural oscillation frequency directly reflects stage gate delay. Fabricating arrays of ring oscillators and localized high-bandwidth voltage droop detectors across varying cell types, metal layers, and supply rails allows characterization teams to measure true local gate delay, dynamic $IR$-drop transients, and intra-die process variation across voltage and temperature, providing ground-truth measurements to calibrate multi-fidelity timing and power models.

Access also needs institutional continuity. Tiny Tapeout and Europractice provide different routes to shared fabrication [@TinyTapeoutRunCatalog; @EuropracticeMPWPrototyping]. Each route depends on the organizations that broker it, as Efabless's closure in early 2025 and Tiny Tapeout's subsequent change of service for SkyWater runs showed [@TinyTapeout2025EfablessShutsDown; @TinyTapeout2025TTSky25aSubmitted]. Maintained tool flows, accepted PDK releases, and published test procedures help preserve a campaign across such changes. Even then, results from separate campaigns become comparable only when the groups agree on the experiment and its baseline.

## Shared Benchmarks and Design Contests {#sec-neutral-governance}

If research groups evaluate different hardware blocks, leave compute hours uncounted, or tune prompts on the test tasks, their reported margins do not answer the same question. The evaluation methods in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect become useful across organizations only when participants agree on tasks, reference baselines, disclosures, and rules for correcting results.

MLCommons and MLPerf provide a precedent for coordinating shared evaluation rules [@MattsonEtAl2020MLPerf]. A working group for architecture automation could maintain reference tasks and tool configurations, require credible baselines, and record when a corrected benchmark requires earlier submissions to be rerun. Independent review and published dispute procedures would prevent any one submitter from controlling the interpretation of its own result.

Separate benchmark divisions could serve different questions. A closed division would compare search methods with fixed tool access and resource budgets. An open division would allow custom methods and tools against the same architectural target, with their costs and dependencies disclosed. Both would report compute, license, and human effort alongside design quality. Neither division's score would establish performance on requirements or workloads the benchmark does not test.

Recurring contests could exercise these rules on problems that need coordinated investigation. The Championship Branch Prediction and Data Prefetching Championship series already provide architecture precedents for shared traces and evaluation rules [@CBP2016BranchPrediction; @DPC2015DataPrefetching]. Possible AI-native design challenges include:

- **Constrained hardware generation.** Entrants translate a high-level specification into register-transfer level (RTL) hardware and carry it through a named implementation flow under a fixed power and thermal budget. Submissions are judged on design quality, the declared checks, and total workflow cost. Passing the contest flow does not authorize commercial tapeout.
- **Sample-efficient design-space exploration.** Teams search microarchitectural configurations across heterogeneous workloads under a strict simulation budget and return the nondominated designs found during the run (those for which no other evaluated candidate is at least as good on every objective and better on at least one). One practical scoring rule measures the fraction of pre-declared target bounds reached within the budget, such as meeting both an energy ceiling and a latency bound while passing all feasibility checks. Reaching those targets tests sample efficiency under fixed goals; it does not show that the run found the true global Pareto frontier.
- **Misleading success and adversarial failures.** Teams seek reward hacking and other cases where an automated workflow improves its reported score without improving the intended hardware outcome. A challenge might expose omitted memory traffic, an unjustified timing exception, or an attempt to alter the evaluator. Red teaming would test the workflow's weaknesses, while seeded faults would supply cases with known answers. Scoring should distinguish detected failures from false alarms and record the checks that exposed them, without treating coverage of the challenge set as proof that no weakness remains.

Unsuccessful submissions retain scientific value after the contest ends. Their inputs and diagnostic logs record which candidate designs broke under the contest constraints and supply material for a shared repository of failed runs.

## Public Repositories of Failed Runs {#sec-open-failed-attempts}

The data chapter established why failed and unresolved runs matter (@sec-data-representations-world-models). Sharing them introduces another problem. A timing violation that is obvious to the originating team may be uninterpretable elsewhere because its constraints are missing, its library is restricted, or its annotation confuses a symptom with a cause. A public repository needs to preserve enough context for a different group to decide how the observation can be used.

Contributors should retain the diagnostic return, inputs, conditions, and dependencies that support each annotation, and state which steps cannot be replayed with public resources. Shared status meanings must keep a design violation separate from an execution failure and a confirmed cause separate from a hypothesis. Those distinctions let a receiving team use a timing failure as a scoped observation without treating a license timeout as a negative hardware example.

Disclosure review must preserve that meaning while protecting confidential designs. Removing cell names and absolute coordinates from a congestion map may make it easier to share, but can also remove information needed to explain the failure. Several released records may reveal a product's geometry even when each looks innocuous alone. Each release should therefore state what was removed and which diagnostic uses remain supported; reliable methods for making that trade-off remain a research problem (@sec-ecosystem-open-questions).

OpenROAD-flow-scripts already publishes test results, logs, and artifacts through its [continuous integration infrastructure](https://openroad-flow-scripts.readthedocs.io/en/latest/contrib/CI.html). A community repository would extend that practice across projects with shared annotations, disclosure review, and maintainers who keep dependencies and interpretations usable as tools change. A static archive alone cannot perform those tasks.

## Sustaining Research and Industrial Adoption {#sec-ecosystem-outlook}

Shared infrastructure requires continuing resources. Someone must update wrappers, maintain reference designs, repair broken dependencies, and review new failure annotations. Research funding that pays only for a first demonstration leaves those costs unassigned. A public release should therefore state who maintains it, which versions are supported, and what access others need to keep it usable.

Commercial tool access presents a related constraint. An automated search may need many parallel tool instances briefly, then none while results are analyzed. Metered licensing can serve that pattern; Synopsys's FlexEDA model, for example, provides by-the-minute cloud access [@Synopsys2022FlexEDA; @Synopsys2026Cloud]. Pricing alone does not determine whether another laboratory can reproduce a study. The license agreement must also permit automated runs, the access the study requires, and publication of comparative results. Sustained tools and clear access terms give students and practitioners a platform on which to develop the engineering skills that automated design still requires.

## Training Architects for AI-Native Design {#sec-curriculum-certification}

Shared records, open implementation flows, and failure repositories change what students can practice. Writing RTL and running individual tools remain essential ways to learn how hardware behaves. Students must also learn to formulate architectural hypotheses, construct alternatives, and determine which parts of that work a learned model can perform. A proposed accelerator gives them two related subjects to investigate: how its organization affects application performance, and how the information and choices available to a model affect the designs it proposes.

An AI-native curriculum therefore extends quantitative architectural reasoning to the design process itself. In one exercise, a student first predicts a bottleneck and proposes a change, then gives an agent a bounded opportunity to investigate the same problem. The student compares the prediction, the agent's proposal, and the measured outcome before changing one part of the automated process, such as the performance counters exposed to the agent. Repeated runs and workloads withheld from development can then test whether the revised process finds useful designs more consistently or at lower total cost. Analytical models and conventional search methods remain comparators throughout.

The stages of the design loop connect those investigations to established architecture skills (@tbl-classical-to-ai-native-skills). Students use the same foundations to improve the proposed hardware and to decide how an automated search should investigate it.

| **Life-cycle stage** | **Foundational skill** | **Use in an AI-native design loop** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Formulate** | Workload characterization and quantitative reasoning | Use traffic, working sets, and precision requirements to define the question, permitted changes, and comparison. |
| **Explore** | Performance bounds and design-space reasoning | Turn analytical bounds into screening checks, then test whether the checks help the search find useful alternatives. |
| **Implement** | Computer arithmetic and microarchitectural organization | Develop compatible datapaths and software schedules, with reference models that test generated implementations. |
| **Evaluate** | Simulation, verification, and physical implementation | Choose checks that can observe the candidate's intended benefits and possible violations. |
| **Interpret** | Experimental attribution and diagnosis | Use controlled contrasts and diagnostic traces to distinguish a measured outcome from its proposed cause. |
| **Commit** | Comparative judgment and responsibility | Weigh design quality, total cost, unresolved checks, and residual risk before recommending the next step. |
: **AI-native design applies architectural foundations to both the hardware and the process that explores it.** The stages of @sec-architecture-20-ontology connect constructive design, experiment selection, and judgment without assuming that a learned method improves the work. {#tbl-classical-to-ai-native-skills tbl-colwidths="[17,30,53]"}

For example, a conservation-of-bytes bound can reject an infeasible memory-traffic proposal before simulation. Structured bottleneck telemetry can then help a search choose which candidate to evaluate, as work on agentic design-space exploration investigates [@WangEtAl2026AgentDSE]. Students must test whether those choices improve the search rather than infer success from a model's explanation; evaluations of hardware-performance reasoning show why simulator feedback matters [@WangEtAl2026ArchEval]. The skill therefore goes beyond calculating bounds and reading bottleneck telemetry. Students must also decide how each should guide the loop and measure what each contributes.

Students also need the diagnostic judgment to take over when automation fails, and they build it by developing and testing designs and inspecting the resulting artifacts. If students see only a final score, they lose opportunities to connect waveform anomalies, timing reports, and congestion maps to the circuit that produced them. Shared teaching artifacts should therefore include the underlying design and diagnostic returns so that students gain the experience needed to investigate failures (@sec-what-architect-owns).

::: {.callout-law title="Bainbridge's Ironies of Automation in Hardware Design"}
**The Classical Principle:** Automating routine tasks can reduce opportunities to maintain the skills needed when the operator must take over. The remaining faults may demand more experience precisely when routine practice has diminished [@Bainbridge1983Ironies].

**Hardware Design Application:** A summary score can report that a candidate failed without teaching the reviewer how to distinguish a layout problem from an incorrect timing constraint. Training must include the underlying artifacts and the checks that separate those causes.

**Mitigation Strategy:** Implement shadow verification audits and diagnostic fault-injection training to restore the operator's exposure to structural debugging without reverting to routine manual drafting (@sec-law-ironies-automation in @sec-appendix-b-laws-paradoxes).
:::

Two laboratory practices can rebuild that diagnostic experience in a setting where mistakes are safe to investigate before fabrication. In a shadow verification audit, a student follows an automated exploration run and forms an independent hypothesis about the bottleneck the optimizer is targeting. The student then audits the generated RTL alongside its Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) declarations and compares that diagnosis against the instructor's review. The student learns by explaining why a reported speedup survives or fails downstream checks rather than merely watching the run finish.

In a companion fault-injection laboratory, instructors seed an unsafe clock-domain crossing, an unhandled reset state, or an unjustified timing exception. Students choose the corresponding structural analysis, simulation or formal check, or constraint audit, and explain what it can and cannot observe (@sec-feedback-verification-trust). Cases from instructor-curated defects and shared failure repositories make that practice available without requiring each class to rediscover the same mistakes.

Instructors can adopt these practices locally; shared, maintained examples let other courses reproduce and extend them. Assessment should examine a student's proposed design, causal explanation, experimental choices, and ability to transfer that reasoning to an unfamiliar workload. The aim is an architect who can build and improve a design loop while recognizing when its evidence is insufficient.

## Open Questions {#sec-ecosystem-open-questions}

The questions that close each chapter mark where established engineering practice gives way to open research. At the community level, those unsolved problems sit where cross-team comparability, physical silicon measurements, and intellectual-property protection pull against one another:

- **When a design wins on an open predictive PDK, when does it still win under commercial foundry signoff?** Academic groups can compare candidates under ASAP7, but access restrictions make matched comparisons with commercial flows difficult. Different cells, wiring rules, and operating conditions can change the ranking. We need coordinated studies that expose where the accessible flow predicts those trade-offs and where it fails, while preserving the commercial information each participant must protect.

- **How can a benchmark consortium audit closed-loop design claims when foundry decks and proprietary models cannot be shared?** Independent reviewers must confirm that the team kept the evaluation criteria fixed, ran a matched baseline, and reported compute, license, and human costs. They must do so even when foundry nondisclosure agreements forbid releasing the process deck or transistor netlist. We still need practical attestation protocols and isolated evaluation environments that let outside auditors verify which tools ran, which constraints were enforced, and how resources were spent without exposing confidential silicon libraries.

- **How can teams share failed physical-design runs without leaking confidential product details or stripping away the signals that surrogates need?** Sharing unroutable floorplans, negative timing slack distributions, and power-grid violations helps cure survivorship bias in training datasets. A series of abandoned layouts, however, can also reveal a company's die dimensions, macro floorplan, and clock-frequency targets. We need graph-anonymization methods and formal privacy guarantees that strip out recognizable product geometry while preserving the local congestion and timing patterns that show a surrogate where physical implementation breaks down.

- **How can we instrument low-cost silicon shuttles at mature nodes so their measurements help calibrate surrogates for modern design search?** Multiplexed educational tiles on 130\ nm and 180\ nm MPW shuttles can bring the cost of a small digital design down to a few hundred dollars. Measurements from those tiles reflect mature-node planar transistors and shared harnesses limited to tens of megahertz, so they cannot directly validate a 3\ W, 3\ nm-class mobile compute subsystem. We still lack standardized on-die test harnesses that combine ring-oscillator arrays, transient voltage-droop monitors, and programmable traffic generators on cheap shuttle tiles. Such harnesses would measure systematically where pre-silicon timing and power models drift from real silicon.

## Summary {#sec-ecosystem-coda}

The MPC79 fabrication story that opened this chapter succeeded because it joined two kinds of work: design rules that individual engineers could apply at their own desks and shared brokering services that let them test what they built in silicon. An AI-native architecture ecosystem needs the same division of labor. A structured record schema pays off when another laboratory's tools can parse it without guesswork, and a shared reference flow pays off when researchers can run the physical checks their claims require. Individual teams can adopt the local engineering practices right away while consortium standards and shared infrastructure take shape. Whether those community investments make claims across organizations genuinely comparable remains an empirical question for the field to test.

::: {.callout-takeaways}
- **Separate local discipline from shared dependencies.** A team can adopt provenance, failure retention, matched baselines, and total-cost accounting now; cross-team comparison, silicon claims, and public rankings additionally depend on shared schemas, fabrication paths, and neutral governance.
- **Prepare records for another reader.** Retain units, versions, status meanings, costs, and dependencies so a collaborator can interpret a run without relying on its author's memory.
- **Keep failures with their context.** Preserve inputs and diagnostic returns, distinguish tool failures from rejected designs, and review disclosure risks before contributing records to a shared repository.
- **Name the implementation path.** Identify which modeled checks a team's open flow supports and what additional process access or fabricated measurements a broader claim would require.
- **Make a comparison reusable.** Version the task, comparator, checks, and workflow costs together so another group can attempt the same comparison and report where it differs.
- **Teach architects to build and improve the loop.** Combine design hypotheses and controlled comparisons with diagnostic practice. Shared artifacts let students construct alternatives, test an automated method's contribution, and recognize what its checks cannot observe.
:::

The questions across this book are starting points for students and practitioners to develop their own. A useful contribution might be a better design representation, a search method that spends fewer tool runs, a check that exposes a misleading result, or a shared flow that lets another laboratory test an idea. Each can make the next investigation more capable when its inputs, reasoning, results, and limits remain available. That cumulative work gives AI-native design a path from isolated demonstrations toward a teachable engineering discipline.
